messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 73
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: QA Engineer
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
- Pcl5: 74

Margaret is seventy-three years old, but her body still remembers the precise weight of a hand on her shoulder. It is a cool Tuesday morning and she sits in the therapy office with her hands folded neatly in her lap, her wedding ring catching the light. Her husband, Edward, waits in the car—she insisted. The drive here took forty minutes of scanning every rearview mirror, counting license plates, checking for any car that followed too long.

She grew up in a small town in the Midwest, the only child of a schoolteacher and a carpenter. Her father was the caregiver who abused her. The abuse started when she was six, and it was never the dramatic beatings you see in movies. It was the quiet, systematic kind: a pinch that left a bruise on her upper arm that she learned to cover with long sleeves even in summer; a slap across the face if she spilled milk; being locked in the basement closet for hours because she asked a question he thought was disrespectful. Once, when she was nine, he grabbed her by the hair and dragged her across the kitchen floor because she had left a cabinet door open. She learned to open cabinets silently, to never let a dish clink against another, to walk on the balls of her feet so no floorboard squeaked. Her mother never intervened—she was afraid, too.

Margaret escaped to a state college on a scholarship, became a QA engineer in her twenties—a job that suited her perfectly. Finding errors in code, logging every anomaly, tracing bugs to their source: this was what she was already trained to do. She could spend hours bent over a test case, repeating the same sequence until the failure happened, because failure was always hiding somewhere. She married Edward at twenty-eight, a gentle man who never raised his voice. She never told him about her father, not the whole truth. When he asked about her family, she said, “We weren’t close,” and he accepted it.

Now she is retired, but she still lives like a QA engineer. Her day follows a strict protocol: wake at six, check the locks on all doors twice, make the bed with hospital corners, eat the same breakfast (oatmeal, black coffee, half a grapefruit). She keeps a written checklist on the kitchen counter: stove off, windows closed, front door deadbolt engaged. If she cannot complete the checklist, or if she is interrupted mid-sequence, she must restart from the beginning. Edward once came home early and found her in the kitchen, retracing her steps to the front door three times. He asked if she was okay. She said she thought she smelled gas.

The flashbacks do not announce themselves. Sometimes a sharp sound—the clatter of a pot lid hitting the tile floor—and she is nine years old again, frozen in the kitchen, waiting for the blow. Her heart drums, her breathing goes shallow, and she grips the edge of the counter until her knuckles are white. The world tilts, and for a full thirty seconds she is not a retired woman in her own home; she is a child paralyzed by the creak of a floorboard. Edward has learned to say her name quietly, to wait until her eyes come back into focus. He does not touch her from behind.

She avoids certain things without thinking: basements, unlocked closets, the sound of a belt being unbuckled. She cannot watch movies where a father hurts a child. She left a dinner party once when a friend mentioned a “firm hand” in parenting—Margaret excused herself to the restroom and stood with her hands on the sink, breathing in a pattern she taught herself as a girl. Inhale for four, hold for four, exhale for four. She is an expert at keeping her face neutral.

At night, she sleeps on the side of the bed closest to the door. She always has. If Edward moves in his sleep, she wakes instantly—fully awake, no grogginess, eyes scanning the dark for the shape of a man. She tells herself she is just a light sleeper. But her body knows.

The PCL-5 score of 74, which the clinician calculated during the initial intake, is a number Margaret will never see. She does not need a number to know that the past is never past. Each morning she checks the locks, traces the same safe pattern, and tries to convince herself that the door is closed—that no one can open it anymore.
